claims.text: The case involves a dispute over the validity of a mortgage assignment and the right of a borrower to assert a defense against a loan servicer.

The Jacksons filed a complaint in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, alleging that Specialized Loan Servicing LLC (SLS) failed to properly assign the mortgage to them.
The district court granted summary judgment in favor of SLS, ruling that the Jacksons had not established a valid defense against the assignment of the mortgage.

The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed the district court's decision, holding that the Jacksons had not met their burden of proof regarding the invalidity of the mortgage assignment.
The Supreme Court granted certiorari to review whether a borrower may assert a defense against a loan servicer based on the invalidity of the mortgage assignment.
The case involves a dispute over the enforceability of an arbitration clause in a securities transaction under the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA)
The lower court ruled that the arbitration clause was unenforceable because the broker failed to provide adequate disclosure of the risks of arbitration

In AT&T Mobility v. Concepcion (2011), the Supreme Court held that the FAA requires courts to enforce arbitration agreements according to their terms, unless a party can show that the agreement is unconscionable

In Stolt-Nielsen S.A. v. AnimalFeeds International Corp. (2010), the Court held that courts may not infer a party's agreement to arbitrate a particular dispute unless the agreement is clear and explicit

In First Options of Chicago, Inc. v. Kaplan (1995), the Court held that the FAA requires courts to enforce arbitration agreements unless there is a valid reason to invalidate them under general contract law
The case involves the interpretation of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, specifically Section 21A, which provides a safe harbor for certain disclosures by employees of public companies.
The lower court ruled that an employee's disclosure of material nonpublic information to the press, without first reporting it to the company, does not qualify for the safe harbor under Section 21A.

In Central Bank of Denver, N.A. v. First Interstate Bank of Denver, N.A. (1994), the Supreme Court held that Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act does not authorize a private right of action against a lender for aiding and abetting a securities fraud.

In Stoner v. United States (1967), the Court held that a person who voluntarily discloses information to the press is not protected by the safe harbor provision of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.

In 2015, the SEC issued a no-action letter stating that an employee who discloses material nonpublic information to the press without first reporting it to the company may still be protected under the safe harbor if the disclosure is made in good faith and not for personal gain.
The case involves a dispute over the enforceability of an arbitration clause in a contract between a consumer and a cable service provider.
The Supreme Court previously held in AT&T Mobility v. Concepcion (2011) that arbitration clauses in consumer contracts are generally enforceable under the Federal Arbitration Act.
In American Express Co. v. Italian Colors Restaurant (2013), the Court upheld the enforceability of arbitration clauses that prevent consumers from pursuing class-action claims.
The lower court ruled that the arbitration clause in this case was unconscionable due to the disparity in bargaining power between the parties.
The Supreme Court has previously emphasized the strong federal policy favoring arbitration in cases involving the Federal Arbitration Act.
The case involves a dispute over the admissibility of a blood alcohol content (BAC) test result in a drunk driving prosecution under the Fourth Amendment
The petitioner, Gregory P. Warger, was arrested for drunk driving and refused a chemical test, but the state later obtained a warrant to administer the test
The respondent, Randy D. Shauers, argued that the warrantless administration of the test violated the Fourth Amendment
In Schmerber v. California (1966), the Supreme Court held that a warrantless blood test is permissible if there is probable cause and exigent circumstances
In Missouri v. McNeely (2013), the Court held that the natural dissipation of alcohol in the bloodstream does not automatically create exigent circumstances justifying a warrantless blood test
In Birchfield v. North Dakota (2016), the Court held that the Fourth Amendment permits warrantless breath tests incident to arrest, but not warrantless blood tests

In 2010, the Supreme Court ruled in Arizona v. United States that federal law preempts state laws regulating immigration, establishing a framework for evaluating conflicts between state and federal law.

In 2013, the Supreme Court struck down Section 4 of the Voting Rights Act in Shelby County v. Holder, holding that the coverage formula was outdated and violated the principle of equal state sovereignty.

In 2014, the Supreme Court ruled in Texas v. United States that the federal government's immigration enforcement policy was not subject to judicial review, emphasizing the executive's broad discretion in immigration matters.

In 2015, the Supreme Court ruled in United States v. Texas that the federal government's immigration enforcement policy was not subject to judicial review, reaffirming the executive's broad discretion in immigration matters.
In 2015, the Supreme Court ruled in Obergefell v. Hodges that the Fourteenth Amendment requires all states to license and recognize same-sex marriages.
The case involves a dispute over the enforceability of an arbitration clause in a contract between Henry Schein, Inc. and Archer and White Sales, Inc.
The lower court ruled that the arbitration clause was unenforceable because the parties had not agreed to arbitrate the issue of whether the clause was enforceable.

In AT&T Mobility v. Concepcion (2011), the Supreme Court held that the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA) requires courts to enforce arbitration agreements according to their terms, unless the agreement is invalid for a reason that applies to all contracts.
In Stolt-Nielsen S.A. v. AnimalFeeds International Corp. (2010), the Court held that a party cannot be compelled to arbitrate a claim unless there is a clear and unmistakable agreement to do so.

In First Options of Chicago, Inc. v. Kaplan (1995), the Court held that the question of whether an arbitration clause is valid is for the court to decide unless the parties clearly and unmistakably provided otherwise.

The case involves a petition for a writ of certiorari to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit regarding the immigration status of Josue Umana-Escobar, a lawful permanent resident who was ordered removed for a drug-related conviction.

The Ninth Circuit affirmed the decision of the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) that Umana-Escobar was removable under 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(II) for being convicted of a controlled substance offense.

The Supreme Court has previously held that the removal of a lawful permanent resident for a drug-related conviction is permissible under 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(II) if the offense is a 'misdemeanor' or 'felony' as defined by federal law.

In Matter of Lozada, 22 I&N Dec. 131 (BIA 1998), the Board of Immigration Appeals held that a lawful permanent resident who has been convicted of a controlled substance offense is removable under 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(II).
The Supreme Court has also held that the Attorney General has broad discretion in determining whether to grant relief from removal, including under 8 U.S.C. § 1158, which governs asylum applications.

In INS v. Cardoza-Fonseca, 480 U.S. 429 (1987), the Court held that the Attorney General has discretion to grant relief from removal to an alien who has been convicted of an aggravated felony, but that such relief is not mandatory.
The case involves a dispute over the interpretation of a trust agreement, specifically the Mutual Benefits Keep Policy Trust.
The petitioner, Acheron Capital, Ltd., asserts that the respondent, Barry Mukamal, as Trustee, has breached his fiduciary duties by mismanaging trust assets.
The respondent argues that the trust documents do not impose a clear fiduciary duty on the trustee and that the petitioner has not demonstrated a direct harm from the alleged mismanagement.
In the case of Restatement (Second) of Trusts § 170 (1959), it is established that a trustee has a duty to act with the care, skill, and caution of a prudent person in managing trust assets.
In the case of In re Marriage of Haines (1982), the court held that a trustee's failure to follow the terms of a trust agreement can constitute a breach of fiduciary duty.
In the case of Telford v. Telford (1998), the court emphasized that the burden of proof lies with the party alleging a breach of fiduciary duty.

In the case of Reed v. Town of Gilbert (2015), the Supreme Court held that a town's sign code was unconstitutional because it discriminated based on the content of the message on the sign.

In the case of United States v. Grace (1983), the Supreme Court upheld a federal law prohibiting the display of the American flag in a manner that could be construed as disreputable, but the Court emphasized that the law was narrowly tailored to prevent flag desecration.

In the case of Wooley v. Maynard (1977), the Supreme Court held that a state could not require the display of the state motto on license plates if it conflicted with an individual's religious beliefs.

In Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992), the Supreme Court held that a state may not impose an undue burden on a woman's right to choose an abortion before fetal viability.
In Gonzales v. Carhart (2007), the Supreme Court upheld the federal Partial-Birth Abortion Ban Act, finding that it did not impose an undue burden on a woman's right to choose an abortion.

In Whole Woman's Health v. Hellerstedt (2016), the Supreme Court struck down a Texas law requiring abortion providers to have admitting privileges at a local hospital and to meet ambulatory surgical center standards, ruling that the law imposed an undue burden on women seeking abortions.

In June Medical Services LLC v. Russo (2020), the Supreme Court ruled that Louisiana's 2014 law requiring abortion providers to have admitting privileges at a local hospital was unconstitutional, as it imposed an undue burden on women seeking abortions before fetal viability.

The Louisiana law at issue in June Medical Services LLC v. Russo required abortion providers to have admitting privileges at a local hospital, similar to the Texas law struck down in Whole Woman's Health v. Hellerstedt.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari in June Medical Services LLC v. Russo to determine whether the Louisiana law requiring abortion providers to have admitting privileges at a local hospital was constitutional under the precedent of Planned Parenthood v. Casey.
The Fair Housing Act (FHA) prohibits discrimination in housing based on race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, or disability.
In Texas v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc. (2015), the Supreme Court held that disparate impact claims are cognizable under the Fair Housing Act.

The Court in Texas v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc. emphasized that the FHA's prohibition on discrimination includes practices that have a discriminatory effect, even if not motivated by discriminatory intent.
In the case of Village of Arlington Heights v. Metropolitan Housing Corp. (1977), the Court established a four-factor test to evaluate whether a challenged action has a discriminatory effect.
The petitioner, Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., alleged that the respondent's housing development practices had a discriminatory effect on minority communities.
The respondent, Lincoln Property Company, argued that their housing development decisions were based on market demand and not on discriminatory intent.
The case involves a collective action brought by employees of Tyson Foods, Inc. alleging that the company violated the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) by failing to pay them for all hours worked.
The district court certified a class of employees under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23, and the court of appeals affirmed that certification.

The Supreme Court previously held in Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes (2011) that a class action may be certified only if the plaintiffs can show that the defendant's policy or practice is a common question of law or fact that will drive the resolution of the case.
In Comcast Corp. v. Behrend (2011), the Court held that a class action may not be certified if the plaintiffs' damages cannot be proven on a class-wide basis.
The Supreme Court has emphasized that the certification of a class action is a highly discretionary decision that is subject to a strong presumption of correctness on appeal.
The case involves a dispute over the interpretation of a contract between MDK Sociedad De Responsabilidad Limitada and Proplant Incorporated entities.
The lower court ruled in favor of Proplant Incorporated, finding that the contract was not breached by the petitioner.
The Supreme Court granted certiorari to review the lower court's interpretation of the contract's terms and the application of state law.
In cases involving contract interpretation, the Supreme Court has generally deferred to the lower court's factual findings unless there is a clear error of law.
The Court has previously held that the interpretation of a contract is a matter of state law, and federal courts should not substitute their own interpretation unless there is a constitutional issue.
The petitioner has argued that the lower court misapplied the principle of contract formation and failed to consider key evidence presented during the trial.
The case involves a challenge to the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) authority to withhold information from the public under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA)

The petitioner, the Department of Homeland Security, argues that the information sought by the respondent, Robert J. MacLean, is exempt from disclosure under FOIA because it involves sensitive national security and law enforcement information
The respondent, Robert J. MacLean, argues that the information he seeks is not exempt from disclosure and that the government has not met its burden to justify withholding it under FOIA

In Department of Justice v. Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press (1989), the Supreme Court held that the government must demonstrate a specific, justifiable reason for withholding information under FOIA
In National Archives and Records Administration v. Favish (2004), the Court held that the government must show that disclosure would harm a specific interest protected by FOIA's exemptions
In EPA v. Mink (1973), the Court held that the government has the burden of proving that information is exempt from disclosure under FOIA
The case involves a dispute over whether Massage Envy Franchising, LLC violated the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) by failing to pay employees for all hours worked.
The plaintiffs, Kathy Haywood and Lia Holt, allege that they were required to work off-the-clock and were not compensated for those hours.
In 2016, the Supreme Court decided Encino Motorcars, LLC v. Navarro, which held that certain employees of car dealerships are exempt from the FLSA's overtime requirements.

In 2015, the Supreme Court decided Hoffman Plastic Compounds, Inc. v. NLRB, which held that an employer's failure to pay wages does not violate the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) if the wages are not withheld in bad faith.
In 2014, the Supreme Court decided United States v. Wang, which upheld the government's interpretation of the FLSA's definition of 'work' and 'hours worked'.

In 2012, the Supreme Court decided Nationwide Biweekly Administrative Corp. v. Darden, which held that employees who are paid a salary for a fixed number of hours are not entitled to overtime pay for additional hours worked.

In AT&T Mobility v. Concepcion (2011), the Supreme Court held that the FAA's mandate to enforce arbitration agreements applies to consumer contracts, and that state laws that disfavor arbitration are invalid if they conflict with the FAA.

In Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis (2018), the Supreme Court held that the FAA requires courts to enforce arbitration agreements that include class-action waivers, even if the employee would otherwise have a right to bring a collective action.

In 2017, the Department of Labor issued a final rule that redefined the definition of an employee under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), which was challenged in court and later vacated by the D.C. Circuit in 2018.

The respondent, Vincent Keith Bell, claims the ordinance is unconstitutionally vague and overbroad, violating the First Amendment

The Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution protects against unreasonable searches and seizures.
In United States v. Jones (2012), the Supreme Court held that attaching a GPS device to a vehicle constitutes a search under the Fourth Amendment.
In United States v. Miller (1976), the Supreme Court held that the Fourth Amendment does not protect information voluntarily disclosed to third parties.
In Smith v. Maryland (1979), the Supreme Court held that individuals have no reasonable expectation of privacy in the numbers they dial on a telephone.
In United States v. Karo (1988), the Supreme Court held that the use of a tracking device on a container of fuel was a search under the Fourth Amendment.
In United States v. Knotts (1983), the Supreme Court held that the use of a beeper to track a suspect's movements in public was not a search under the Fourth Amendment.
The petitioner, Paul Shifflett, is a state prisoner at SCI Graterford, Pennsylvania, who alleged that he was denied adequate medical care by correctional health staff.
The case involves claims under the Eighth Amendment, which prohibits cruel and unusual punishment, including the denial of medical care.
In Estelle v. Gamble (1976), the Supreme Court held that deliberate indifference to a prisoner's serious medical needs constitutes cruel and unusual punishment.
In Farmer v. Brennan (1994), the Court clarified that a prison official can be liable for deliberate indifference if they knew of and disregarded an excessive risk to the prisoner's health.
In Wilson v. Seiter (1994), the Court held that a prisoner must show that prison officials acted with a sufficiently culpable state of mind to violate the Eighth Amendment.
In Farmer v. Brennan, the Court emphasized that the standard for deliberate indifference is not a negligence standard, but a more stringent one requiring proof of a substantial risk of harm.

In the case of Shifflett v. Korszniak, the lower court found that the petitioner had presented sufficient evidence to suggest that his medical needs were not properly addressed by the correctional health staff.

In Employment Division v. Smith (1990), the Supreme Court held that the Free Exercise Clause does not require the government to accommodate a person's religious practices if the law is neutral and generally applicable.

In Church of Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah (1993), the Supreme Court struck down a city ordinance that prohibited animal sacrifice, holding that the law was not neutral and not generally applicable because it targeted a specific religious practice.
In 2014, the Arkansas Department of Corrections prohibited inmates from growing beards for religious reasons, citing safety and security concerns.
Gregory Houston Holt, an inmate at the Cummins Unit in Arkansas, requested to grow a beard for religious reasons, citing his faith as a Muslim.

In 2014, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit ruled in Holt v. Hobbs (2014) that the Arkansas Department of Corrections' policy violated the Free Exercise Clause because it was not neutral and not generally applicable.
The case involves a challenge to the constitutionality of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) and its implementation by the Department of Justice.
The petitioner, Morshed Alam, is a lawful permanent resident who was denied a visa renewal based on the Attorney General's discretionary authority under the INA.

In INS v. Cardoza-Fonseca (1985), the Supreme Court held that the Attorney General's discretionary authority under the INA must be exercised in a manner consistent with the statutory text and the principle of due process.
In Chevron U.S.A., Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc. (1984), the Court established that courts must defer to agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes, provided they are reasonable.

In Matter of Wang, 21 I&N Dec. 550 (BIA 1996), the Board of Immigration Appeals held that the Attorney General's discretionary authority under the INA is not unlimited and must be exercised in a manner that does not violate constitutional protections.

In Matter of L-O-V-, 27 I&N Dec. 504 (BIA 2018), the Board of Immigration Appeals reaffirmed that the Attorney General's discretion must be exercised in a manner consistent with the statutory framework and constitutional principles.
The case involves a challenge to the constitutionality of a state law that prohibits the use of lethal injection in executions if the method would cause substantial pain and suffering
The petitioner, William Andrew Wright, is a death row inmate who argues that the state's execution method violates the Eighth Amendment's prohibition on cruel and unusual punishment
In Glossip v. Gross (2015), the Supreme Court upheld the use of lethal injection as a constitutional method of execution, rejecting a similar challenge based on the risk of pain
In Baze v. Rees (2008), the Court held that the use of lethal injection does not violate the Eighth Amendment, provided that the method is not deliberately designed to cause pain
The petitioner's argument relies on the claim that the state's execution protocol is unconstitutionally risky due to the potential for botched executions
In 2019, the Supreme Court had not yet ruled on a case involving the specific issue of whether a state's execution method is unconstitutionally risky due to the potential for pain

The petitioner, Adaucto Chavez-Mesa, was convicted under the ACCA based on a prior state conviction for assault with a deadly weapon.

In United States v. Taylor (1990), the Supreme Court held that a state offense qualifies as a 'violent felony' under the ACCA if it has as an element the use, attempted use, or threatened use of physical force against another person.
In Begay v. United States (2007), the Court held that a state offense is not a 'violent felony' under the ACCA if it is a general intent crime, even if it involves the use of a dangerous weapon.

In Johnson v. United States (2015), the Court struck down the residual clause of the ACCA, which had allowed for the inclusion of offenses that 'involve conduct that presents a serious potential risk of physical injury to another.'
The case involves a challenge to the constitutionality of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) and its application to noncitizens seeking relief from removal.
The petitioner is a noncitizen who was placed in removal proceedings and seeks relief under the INA.
The respondent is the Attorney General, who is responsible for enforcing the INA and making decisions on immigration matters.

The Supreme Court has previously held that the INA provides a comprehensive framework for immigration enforcement and that courts generally defer to the Attorney General's interpretation of the statute.

In INS v. Cardoza-Fonseca (1985), the Court held that the Attorney General has discretion to grant relief from removal in certain circumstances, including hardship to a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident.

In Matter of Lozada, 22 I&N Dec. 1102 (BIA 1999), the Board of Immigration Appeals held that an alien who is not a lawful permanent resident may not be eligible for cancellation of removal based on hardship to a U.S. citizen spouse.
The Court has also recognized that the Attorney General's discretion in immigration matters is broad and that courts should not substitute their own judgment for that of the agency.

The Social Security Act provides for disability benefits to individuals who are unable to engage in any substantial gainful activity due to a medically determinable physical or mental impairment that is expected to result in death or last for a continuous period of not less than 12 months.

In Richardson v. Perales (1978), the Supreme Court held that the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare must provide a full and fair hearing to a claimant seeking disability benefits, and that the Secretary's decision must be supported by substantial evidence.

In Bowen v. City of New York (1986), the Supreme Court held that the Secretary's decision to deny disability benefits must be based on a proper application of the law and the evidence, and that the Secretary must consider all relevant evidence, including medical opinions and the claimant's daily activities.

In Sullivan v. Zebley (1989), the Supreme Court held that the Secretary must evaluate a child's disability under the same standards as an adult, and that the Secretary must consider the child's ability to function in a work-like setting.

In Barnhart v. Thomas (2000), the Supreme Court held that the Secretary's decision must be based on a consideration of the entire record, and that the Secretary must not rely solely on the opinion of a single medical source.

In Social Security Ruling 06-03p, the Social Security Administration provided guidance on the evaluation of mental disorders, emphasizing the importance of considering the claimant's ability to function in daily life and the consistency of the claimant's symptoms with the medical evidence.

The case involves a dispute over the statute of limitations for patent infringement under 35 U.S.C. § 286
The United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit held that the statute of limitations for patent infringement is six years from the date of the infringing act

In the case of SCA Hygiene Products Aktiebolag v. First Quality Baby Products, LLC, the Supreme Court was asked to determine whether the statute of limitations for patent infringement is six years from the date of the infringing act or from the date the patent was issued
The Supreme Court previously held in American Pipe & Construction Co. v. Utah (1974) that the statute of limitations for patent infringement begins to run when the infringing act occurs

In the case of SCA Hygiene Products Aktiebolag v. First Quality Baby Products, LLC, the petitioner argued that the statute of limitations should begin to run from the date of the infringing act, not the date the patent was issued
The respondent argued that the statute of limitations should begin to run from the date the patent was issued, citing the language of 35 U.S.C. § 286

The Supreme Court granted certiorari to determine whether the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) allows for expedited removal of aliens who are not lawful permanent residents and who are apprehended within 14 days of entry into the United States.

The INA provides that an alien who is not a lawful permanent resident and who is apprehended within 14 days of entry may be removed without a hearing if the alien is determined to be inadmissible under certain provisions of the INA.
In INS v. Lopez-Mendoza (1984), the Supreme Court held that the expedited removal process under the INA does not require a hearing or an opportunity to be heard before removal.

In Sale v. Haitian Centers Council (1993), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of the expedited removal process, emphasizing that the INA's procedures for removal are not subject to the same procedural safeguards as those for deportation.

In Matter of L-O- (1996), the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) interpreted the INA to allow for expedited removal of aliens who are not lawful permanent residents and who are apprehended within 14 days of entry.

The petitioner argued that the INA's expedited removal provisions are consistent with the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and do not violate due process because they are not subject to the same procedural requirements as formal deportation proceedings.

The respondent argued that the expedited removal process violates the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause because it denies the alien an opportunity to present evidence or challenge the basis for removal.
